results.title: representations, we introduce a permutation annealing strategy that gradually transitions from full permutation to natural sequential order. This three-stage approach is controlled by two hyperparameters: *start* and *end*, defining the annealing period. The training process follows a progressive annealing schedule: initially, the model undergoes full permutation training to learn position-invariant knowledge representations; during the annealing phase (from *start* to *end* epochs), the permutation probability gradually decreases, allowing the model to begin integrating scattered knowledge fragments. Finally, the model focuses exclusively on natural sequential order to consolidate the learned knowledge into coherent representations. We systematically analyze the impact of different annealing schedules on model performance across the NovelHuman dataset. Detailed experimental results comparing various *start* and *end* configurations are presented in Table C3 of Appendix C.3. Our findings demonstrate that this progressive annealing strategy significantly enhances novel knowledge acquisition, with optimal performance achieved when models undergo substantial full permutation training followed by gradual transition and focused sequential consolidation. This three-stage approach effectively transforms dispersed knowledge fragments into comprehensive, coherent representations.

item.text: {"text":"Recent work supports probing temporal dependence, but unrestricted shuffling has interpretive limits. [Does It Look Sequential? (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.12008) compares original and shuffled histories across 15 datasets, finding weak sequential structure in several popular benchmarks. [IDEA (SIGIR 2025)](https://le-wu.com/files/Publications/CONFERENCES/SIGIR25-IDEA.pdf) highlights distribution shifts and warns that arbitrary augmentations can discard informative interactions or preserve noise. Together, these motivate a distinction: sensitivity to perturbed histories alone does not establish useful temporal reasoning; perturbations may also change history plausibility.\n\nThe statistical foundation is older: [Berrett et al.’s conditional permutation test](https://academic.oup.com/jrsssb/article/82/1/175/7056014) samples nonuniform permutations that preserve dependence on observed confounders; calibration depends on the estimated conditional distribution. A proposed adaptation—not an established recommendation-specific test—is to match training-history replacements on prefix length, item-frequency bins, title/description similarity and repetition, then compare local swaps at different distances from the final interaction. Report matching coverage, covariate imbalance, transition-support rates and paired target-rank/top-10 changes, stratified by perturbation distance and support. Preserve padding and optionally fix the latest item to isolate earlier-order effects. Treat these as descriptive sensitivity diagnostics unless conditional sampling assumptions justify formal p-values; neither matching nor rank changes establish causality. Reuse one frozen NextItNet per category, derive matches only from public training data, and keep diagnostic results separate from pinned macro validation HR@10. The located sources do not establish this exact matched-history protocol as a standard 2024–2026 method."}
